title: 30 US Senators Flag Visa Appointment Delays Affecting Thousands of Indian Students
excerpt: A bipartisan group of senators has urged the State Department to address growing backlogs that threaten to prevent Indian students from starting the fall semester at American universities.
body:
• Thirty US senators have written to the State Department flagging significant delays in student visa appointments that disproportionately affect Indian students
  • Indian students are the largest group of international students in the US, contributing an estimated $9 billion annually to the American economy
  • The delays come after a three-week freeze on new F, J, and M visa appointments earlier this summer and the recent four-year cap on student visa stays
  • Multiple bipartisan congressional efforts have now urged the administration to prioritize visa processing as fall semester enrollment deadlines approach

Thirty US senators have raised the alarm over persistent delays in student visa appointments that are threatening to derail the academic plans of thousands of Indian students heading to American universities this fall.

The bipartisan group wrote to the State Department urging it to address the growing backlogs at US consulates in India, where students have reported checking online portals multiple times daily in hopes of securing interview slots with no guarantee of timely appointments.

A Pattern of Mounting Delays

The senators' letter is the latest in a series of escalating congressional interventions. In July 2025, Congresswoman Deborah Ross led a bipartisan group of 14 House members — including Indian American representatives Pramila Jayapal, Raja Krishnamoorthi, and Shri Thanedar — in writing to Secretary of State Marco Rubio about the same issue.

"Indian students form the largest group of international students in the United States and contribute $9 billion annually to the U.S. economy. We are dismayed at the possibility that many of these bright young individuals may be blocked from continuing their education and research in the United States."

— Congressional letter to the State Department

That letter followed a nearly month-long freeze on new student visa appointments by the Trump administration earlier in the summer of 2025, which threw travel plans into chaos for students who had already secured admissions and paid deposits.

Policy Shifts Compound the Problem

The visa backlogs are occurring against a backdrop of significant policy changes. In July 2026, the Department of Homeland Security published a rule capping international student stays at four years, replacing the decades-old "duration of status" framework that had allowed students to remain as long as needed to complete their programs.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the change allows the government to "properly screen, vet, and monitor individuals within our borders." But educators and immigration advocates have pushed back strongly.

NAFSA, the association of international educators, called it "a misguided and unnecessary policy shift that injects uncertainty, bureaucracy, and fear into a system that has long worked effectively." The proposed rule attracted more than 15,700 public comments, the overwhelming majority in opposition.

Economic Stakes Are High

The delays carry significant economic implications. International students contributed $44 billion to the US economy in the 2023-2024 academic year, and for every three international students, one American job is created or supported, according to the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration.

Indian student enrollment in the US has already fallen 6.9% amid tighter scrutiny and the four-year visa cap, according to recent data. Research universities are particularly concerned, as graduate programs in science, technology, engineering, and artificial intelligence depend heavily on Indian students.

What Comes Next

The US Embassy in India continues to warn that timely visa appointments cannot be guaranteed. With fall semester start dates just weeks away, the senators are pressing for emergency measures including expanded interview slots, increased staffing at Indian consulates, and broader use of virtual interviews and waivers.

For the estimated 200,000-plus Indian students enrolled across American universities, the coming weeks will determine whether bureaucratic bottlenecks turn acceptance letters into deferred dreams.
